To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
people's metacognitive judgments are experience based, but they also have an information base.
people are generally better at predicting their performance on a given task when they rely on information about the task and the stimuli, rather than on their own experience with the task.

(1) the use of information about the learning environment is the main factor that determines the quality of JOLs and FOKs, (2) the use of experience based information is the main factor determining the accuracy of JOLs, and (3) the use of EB information is the main determinant of FOKs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how people know what they know, and the answer we offer is that there are two modes of knowing.
the question of what people know about what they know.
the question of how people monitor the contents of their minds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that the IB and the EB systems are two distinct systems that operate in parallel, and are activated simultaneously in the process of monitoring (Koriat et al., 2006).
the evidence from the literature is consistent with the idea that metacognitive judgments are based on both information based and experience based processes.

the dual process framework is not only an important theoretical perspective in its own right, but also an extremely valuable conceptual tool in the analysis of metacommonly referred to as metacognition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
people can use both types of processes to monitor their knowledge and that they can use them either separately or in combination.

experience based and information based metacognitive monitoring processes have different effects, which depend on whether people are asked to predict their future performance (JOLs), to report their current performance (FOKs), or to make a retrospective assessment (RJOLs) In addition, we show that the effects of experience based and information driven metacognitive processes depend on the type of task and on the type of metacognitive judgment.
experience based metacognition is a good thing, whereas information based metacognition can be a bad thing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distinction between the two processes is not a mere matter of theoretical convenience, but rather a distinction that is reflected in the very architecture of human cognition.
the two processes are not necessarily in conflict, but rather can be complementary and can even be used in tandem to improve the accuracy of metacognitive judgments.
the two types of processes can have opposite effects on metacognitive monitoring and on metacognitive control.
